payload.title: What Are the Filipino Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s, often with a Filipino partner, parent or grandparent, who are planning or attending a wedding with Filipino roots (in the Philippines or elsewhere) and want to know what each custom means, who the sponsors are and what they do, and what marrying legally in the Philippines involves for Australians.
payload.goal: Read the free Wedded Wonderland digital magazine (primary CTA); secondary, in-context invitation to speak with a Wedded Advisor placed straight after the legal section on marrying in the Philippines.
payload.service_link: /magazine (primary, UTM-tagged); /wonderland-concierge (secondary, UTM-tagged, after the legal section)
payload.angle: Page-one listicles (and our own old page) mix church rites, pre-colonial history and superstitions into one undifferentiated list resting on anecdote. We group customs by when they happen (before the day, the ceremony, the reception), explain who does what (principal and secondary sponsors, and which sponsor handles the coins, candles, veil and cord), separate sourced meaning from what is only 'often told', note that not every Filipino wedding is Catholic, and add what Australians need and listicles skip: Smartraveller's current Philippines advice levels and where higher levels apply, plus the legal steps to marry in the Philippines from official sources only. It is the Filipino chapter of our sourced wedding traditions pillar.
must_include: Exactly 4 one-sentence Key takeaways at the top.
10 to 12 customs from tradition_plan, grouped before the day, the ceremony, the reception, each with a sourced meaning; unsourced origins labelled 'often told' or left out.
A sponsors explainer (principal sponsors ninong and ninang; secondary sponsors for candle, veil and cord; coin and ring bearers only if sourced).
A line that customs vary by region and faith (Catholic, other Christian, Muslim Filipino, Indigenous communities), with specific variation only where sourced.

A legal section for Australians marrying in the Philippines, sourced to Smartraveller, the Australian Embassy Manila or Philippine government pages only; 'a fee applies' for any fee; anything unconfirmed becomes 'check with the local civil registrar'.

Smartraveller's overall level (Exercise a high degree of caution) with the page date, the higher-level regions named, and a prompt to check Smartraveller before booking; any destination suggestion sits outside higher-level regions.
Internal link to the pillar /expert-advice/wedding-traditions in the intro and the close.
Short FAQ (5 to 6 questions) from SEO People Also Ask, sourced answers only; primary CTA /magazine, secondary Wedded Advisor CTA after the legal section; Advisor claims only from brand-facts.md.

tradition_plan.note: Planner fact-checks in 2 parallel batches with separate scratch folders, 15 min hard, no extra sourcing rounds. Preferred sources: National Commission for Culture and the Arts (ncca.gov.ph), National Museum of the Philippines, Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines or archdiocesan pages for church rites, Britannica, academic or university sources. Legal: Smartraveller, Australian Embassy Manila (philippines.embassy.gov.au), Philippine Statistics Authority, Philippine government pages. Not found in time: 'often told' or drop.

facts_to_source: What it is and who attends
Meaning of the word (from panhik, to go up) only if sourced
Food or gifts brought, and what is discussed (date, arrangements)
Harana (serenading during courtship): mention only if sourced, as historic or rural

batch_A.tradition: Despedida de soltera (farewell party for the bride)
facts_to_source: What it is, who hosts, when
Spanish-origin name and meaning
Any groom equivalent only if sourced

facts_to_source: Principal sponsors: role as witnesses and mentors
Secondary sponsors: candle, veil and cord pairs
Whether principal sponsors sign the marriage certificate as witnesses (legal claim: Philippine government source or drop)

Meaning: provision and shared prosperity

Candle sponsors light candles on either side of the couple
Meaning in the rite
'Candle blowing out' superstition: often told or drop
Veil placed over the bride's head and the groom's shoulders
Meaning (two clothed as one)
Cord placed in a figure eight over the couple after the veil

Meaning (bond of marriage)

batch_A.tradition: Superstitions before the day (sukob, not trying on the gown, no sharp gifts)
facts_to_source: Sukob: siblings not marrying in the same year (source or 'often told')
Bride not trying on the gown before the day
Knives or sharp objects as gifts

batch_B.tradition: Rice or petal shower as the couple leave
facts_to_source: Rice thrown for abundance and fertility
Petals as an alternative, only if sourced

No amounts

facts_to_source: Barong tagalog: embroidered shirt, fabrics such as pina or jusi
Filipiniana and terno (butterfly sleeves); baro't saya as the older form
Prefer NCCA or National Museum sources

batch_B.tradition: Legal section: Australians marrying in the Philippines
facts_to_source: Certificate of legal capacity to contract marriage for foreign nationals: what it is and who issues it for Australians (Australian Embassy Manila)
Marriage licence from the local civil registrar; any waiting or posting period (Philippine government source)
Documents commonly needed (passport, birth certificate) only if stated
Whether a church wedding is legally valid when solemnised by an authorised officiant
Registering the marriage and the PSA certificate
Fees: 'a fee applies'; timelines only if sourced; otherwise 'check with the local civil registrar' and a [[VERIFY]]
Smartraveller levels from 02-research/pages/smartraveller.md (already fetched; do not re-fetch)

optional_if_sourced: Wedding feast and lechon (no vendor names)
Muslim Filipino customs (e.g. Maranao or Tausug weddings) from NCCA or academic sources only, as culture, never paired with travel to higher-level regions
Bride stepping on the groom's foot, rain as luck (fold into superstitions)
dropped_from_old_page: Priest drawing blood from the couple's chests: sensational, unsourced; drop unless a museum or academic source supports it as historic
Three-day wedding as a current norm: unsourced; history only if sourced
Dropping the ring means death or misery: drop
FAQ 'Candle, Veil and Cord are the only bridesmaids required': unsourced
'Colonised by the Spanish in the 18th Century': wrong, do not repeat

avoid: Reusing wording, structure, quotes or image captions from the old page.
Presenting every custom as Catholic; stereotypes about family size, cost or who pays.
Suggesting any area under Smartraveller Level 3 or 4 (central, western and eastern Mindanao other than Camiguin, Dinagat and Siargao; Sulu Archipelago; southern Sulu Sea).
Prices, fee figures, gift amounts, vendor or venue names.
Legal advice beyond official sources; never guess documents, fees or waiting periods.
Advisor claims beyond brand-facts.md; AI images of people, dress, ceremonies or places.
Competitor branding or copy; em dashes; US spelling; pasted keywords in brackets in headings.
